title: Mahchongitchuge
summary: Mahchongitchuge is a Montauk North Neck swamp name recorded from the 1670 deed for the land between the ponds. The deed places it in a boundary sequence running through the swamp toward Great Pond.
address_label: General North Neck swamp area between Fort Pond and Great Pond / Lake Montauk
map_geometry_source: Approximate/general point in the Montauk North Neck corridor between Fort Pond and Great Pond/Lake Montauk, offset from Chebiakinnausuk and Gunnunks for map visibility; not an exact swamp boundary.
translation_content:
The first part of Mahchongitchuge is read as connected with a swamp. Two possible readings are offered for the ending: a place of rushes, or a place of separation or turning place. Because the swamp functioned as a boundary mark, the place-of-separation reading fits the record.

Why Place Names Matter

“Place names are everywhere. We use them so often that it’s easy not to think about them. But each name tells a story. Often, these stories have replaced other stories. Learning about these stories can teach us a lot about our history and our values.”

— New Zealand Ministry of Education, Tūranganui-a-Rua, Tūranganui-a-Maru, Tūranganui-a-Kiwa e! (2022), ‘What’s in a name?’ sidebar, PDF page 7 (viewer page 5)

Place-name history should show Native people as active and present, not only as names in old documents.
land_loss_content: Mahchongitchuge shows how wetlands served as named boundary places in Montaukett land records. Recording it alongside nearby North Neck names helps reconstruct a connected Indigenous geography of ponds, swamps, ridges, and deed lines.
whereintheworld_content: The map placement is a general point in the Montauk North Neck corridor between Fort Pond and Great Pond, now Lake Montauk, not the exact hay-stack swamp location described in the 1670 deed.
